 Statistical arbitrage. A hedge fund classic. Explained with a dog. This is a man walking his dog. The man is what a stock should cost. The dog is what it actually costs. The dog runs ahead. The dog falls behind. But there is a leash. So sooner or later, it comes back. And that is the whole trade. Dog too far ahead, you sell the dog and buy the man. Too far behind, you do the opposite. Then you wait. You never bet on where they are going. Up hill, downhill, into traffic. Only on the gap. To run this for real, you need three things. One, an owner for every dog. In practice, a basket of similar stocks. Two, a way to read the leash. Three, a rule for how much to bet. For years, the reading was one assumption. The leash is a spring. Stretch it past a line and it snaps back. A lovely model. It has simply never met a squirrel. The dog keeps going. The model keeps betting it won't. So three researchers at Stanford stopped telling the model how a dog behaves. They gave a neural network 30 days of leash and let it find the shapes itself. First, it looks at a few days at a time and learns small shapes. Up, down, a turn. Then it looks at the whole month at once and decides which days matter. That part is a transformer like the chatbots. The last piece turns that into a bet. Buy or sell and how much for about 550 stocks and it is never graded on predicting prices. Only on steady profit. They tested it on the largest American stocks for 15 years on days it had never seen. The spring model scored about one. A smarter, fixed formula about two. The network scored just over four. Four is the sort of number that makes other quants ask to see your code. And the edge did not come from choosing the owner. It came from how well you read the leash. When they looked inside, the network had taught itself an old market saying, markets take the escalator up and the elevator down. Now, the fine print. That four is before trading costs. After them, it is about one. Still profitable, slightly less magical. But in 15 years, the profit never faded, which suggests it is not free money. It is a wage for pulling prices back into line. Somebody has to hold the leash. The paper is 68 pages. This was three minutes. You're welcome.
